rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Machine-cadence fat — the shape of good prose without the content.
rules_evaluated.evidence: (a) Empty negation: closest is L46 'if two sessions open the same working directory (not two worktrees, the same folder)' — this negates a real, plausible misreading (that the trap is about separate worktree folders), so it is a needed disambiguation, not an empty one. (b) Deictic drumroll: L29 'That creates a sibling directory...' and L74 'This is the one place the human stays in the driver seat' both resolve a real antecedent (the command shown; the conflict-recovery moment just described) — legitimate per the rule's own test (can you point at what it refers to? yes to both). (c) Bold-label echo: L19/21/23 '**Branches** are cheap.' / '**Clones** are heavy.' / '**Worktrees** are the middle path.' — the bold word is the sentence's own subject, not a restated label followed by a new sentence repeating the noun (the banned 'Acceptance Tests. Acceptance tests define…' shape); not an echo. (d) Citation/appendix duplication: no Sources block or repeated inline gloss in body.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Don't state a count the adjacent list already holds.
rules_evaluated.evidence: L17: 'Three ways to have "another copy of this code to work on." They behave differently.' sits directly above the three bold-lead paragraphs that follow (Branches / Clones / Worktrees) — the exact banned shape. The sibling instance of this rule, formerly at L80 ('Three situations where one session beats three.'), has been fixed in this file as of the pinned diff (now reads 'Situations where one session beats three.'), confirming the pattern is recognized and fixable without loss; this second instance was named as the weaker/secondary case in the prior pass and was left unfixed. The numeral is never reused as a memory handle elsewhere in the file, so the across-distance carve-out doesn't rescue it — the items are visible in the very next lines. Harm: a fourth means of duplicating a repo added later (e.g. sparse-checkout) silently falsifies 'Three', and the drift is invisible to an editor working on the list, not the sentence above it.
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: Drop the numeral: 'Ways to have "another copy of this code to work on." They behave differently.'

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: A slogan that is false as stated is not punchy framing — run the truth test before reaching for §12.
rules_evaluated.evidence: L11: 'Nothing silently overwrites.' is stated as an unqualified absolute directly after the merge-collision sentence ('If two sessions collide, Git tells you at merge time.'), but the file's own next section (L46, 'The agent-level trap') describes a real silent overwrite Git does nothing to prevent: two sessions writing into the same working directory — not a git operation at all, a raw filesystem clobber — where 'the later write wins' and 'the earlier session's in-progress edit gets clobbered on disk' with no warning surfaced to either session. The cheapest counterexample is the file's own next section, exactly the diagnostic the rule names ('the curriculum's own contingency plan'). A charitable reading scopes L11 to committed, merge-tracked work, but the sentence as written carries no such scoping, and a precise engineer reader finds the tension faster than the author did. Fix would not degrade the artefact — a short scoping clause, not a rewrite.
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: Scope the claim, e.g. 'If two sessions collide on committed work, Git tells you at merge time — nothing silently overwrites there' — so it isn't read against the same-directory clobber described 35 lines later.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Golden path only in body — THIS RULE HAS AN EXCEPTION; read to the boundary before cutting anything.
rules_evaluated.evidence: The file's entire back half is recovery content by design ('Conflict recovery when two sessions edited the same file', 'When NOT to run multi-session') — this is squarely inside the rule's own boundary: a plausible failure (merge collisions and mis-scoped parallelism are the expected failure modes of the exact workflow being taught) with a non-obvious rescue (don't let the agent auto-resolve; read the diff yourself), stated as one tight passage next to the risk, not routed to a maintainer-only or live-support surface a student in delivery never reaches. The title itself frames the whole file as a 'survival guide' — recovery is the golden path here, not an aside to it.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Don't ask student to manually diff or spot-check Claude's output as error-catching.
rules_evaluated.evidence: L74-76's 'Read the diff. Pick which line wins, or write the line that reconciles both.' names both object (the diff — exempt per the rule's own example, 'the diff is the artifact') and tell (pick or write the reconciling line), and states the reason it can't be delegated ('agents are confident and do not always read carefully enough at a merge boundary'). This isn't error-catching on the agent's output (checking whether the agent got something wrong); it's a two-sided git conflict where both changes may be legitimate and only the human knows intent — a different task the rule doesn't ban. No un-addressed speech verb (say/name/quote/tell/flag), no bare 'name X' imperative, no attitude-adverb standing in for an action, no unknowable criterion, no fictional 'must/every X' gate — every imperative in body names a doable, checkable action.

Stays inside; flagged as the closest call in the file.
